Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 70, verse 1:

(p-29) Surah al-Ma'arij is Meccan, and its verses number forty-four.

﴿A petitioner asked﴾, that is: a caller called out.

﴿for a punishment that will befall﴾, that is: he sought it and demanded it. This was al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, when he said, in denial and mockery: ﴿If this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky, or bring us a painful punishment.﴾ It was also said that it was Abu Jahl, when he said: ﴿Then cause pieces of the sky to fall upon us.﴾ It was also said that it was al-Harith ibn al-Nu'man al-Fihri. The reason was that when he heard the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about Ali (may Allah be pleased with him): "Whoever I am his mawla, Ali is his mawla," he said: "O Allah, if what Muhammad says is true, then rain down upon us stones from the sky." He had not waited long before Allah the Exalted struck him with a stone, which fell upon his brain and came out through his lower part, and he died on the spot. It was also said that it was the Messenger (ﷺ) who asked for their punishment to be hastened.

It was recited as (sa'ala), and this is either from su'al (asking) in the dialect of Quraysh, so the meaning is as already mentioned, or it is from sayalan (flowing). This is supported by its being recited as (sala sayl), that is: a valley gushed forth ﴿with a punishment that will befall﴾. The past-tense form is used to indicate the certainty of its occurrence, either in this world, and this is the punishment of the Day of Badr, since al-Nadr was killed on that day by being held and executed; the condition of al-Fihri has already been mentioned; or in the Hereafter, and this is the punishment of the Fire. And Allah knows best.

This is the commentary of Abu al-Su'ud on Surah 70 (al-Ma'arij), verse 2, from his work Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim (Guidance of the Sound Intellect).

﴿لِلْكافِرِينَ﴾ is another attributive qualifier of "ʿadhāb" (a punishment), meaning: "belonging to the disbelievers." Alternatively, it is a complement (ṣilah) of "wāqiʿ" (befalling), or it is connected to "saʾala" (asked), meaning: he called down, for the disbelievers, a punishment that will befall them. His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿لَيْسَ لَهُ دافِعٌ﴾ ("there is none to avert it") is another attributive qualifier of "ʿadhāb," or a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) from it, since it is specified by the attribute or by the action; or it is a circumstantial qualifier from the pronoun in "al-kāfirīn" on the assumption that it is an attribute of "ʿadhāb"; or it is a new, independent sentence (istiʾnāf).

"From Allah" is connected either to "will befall" or to "will repel," meaning: there is no repeller of it from His side, exalted is He.

"Owner of the ascents": the ascents by which the angels climb, carrying the commands and prohibitions; or it refers to the heavens arranged one above another.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 70, verse 4:**

﴿The angels and the Spirit ascend to Him﴾. That is, Jibril (peace be upon him) is singled out for mention because of his distinction and excellence. It has also been said that "the Spirit" is a kind of creature who are guardians over the angels, just as the angels are guardians over people.

﴿to Him﴾: to His Throne, may He be exalted, and to the place from which His commands descend, may He be exalted. It has also been said that this is of the same kind as the words of Ibrahim (peace be upon him): "Indeed I am going to my Lord" (Qur'an 37:99), meaning: to the place to which He has commanded me.

﴿in a Day whose measure is fifty thousand years﴾ by the reckoning of people. This explains the extent of the height of those ascent-paths and the vastness of their reach, in the manner of figurative representation and imagery. The meaning is that they are so high that, if their crossing were measured in time, that time would equal fifty thousand years of the years of this world. It has also been said that the meaning is: the angels and the Spirit ascend to His Throne, may He be exalted, in a Day whose measure is like the measure of fifty thousand years, that is: they cover in one day what a human being would cover in fifty thousand years, if that were assumed. It has also been said that "in a Day" is connected to *waqi'* (ﻭاقِع, "about to occur"). It has also been said that it is connected to *sa'ala* (سَألَ, "asked"), on the assumption that it derives from *al-sayalan* (السَّيَلانِ, "flowing"). In that case, the intended Day is the Day of Resurrection and its prolongation, either because it is truly so, or because of its severity upon the disbelievers, or because of the great number of events and reckonings that occur in it. In any case, that applies to the disbeliever. As for the believer, it does not, because of what Abu Sa'id al-Khudri (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated: that it was said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "How long this Day is!" He (ﷺ) said, "By Him in whose hand my soul is, it will be made light for the believer, until it is lighter for him than an obligatory prayer that he prays in this world."

And His, may He be exalted, saying:

﴿So be patient with a beautiful patience﴾ is connected (*mutaʿallaq*, grammatically dependent) to "سَألَ" (*saʾala*, "asked"), because the question was about mockery, obstinate defiance and denial of the revelation (*wahy*), and that is among the things that would distress him, peace be upon him. Or it was a question born of impatience and urgency for victory. Or it is connected to "سَألَ سائِلٌ" (*saʾala sāʾilun*, "a questioner asked"), or to "سالَ سَيْلٌ" (*sāla saylun*, "a torrent flowed"). Its meaning then is: the punishment has come, because its occurrence is near, for you have nearly reached the vengeance.

﴿Indeed they see it﴾, that is, the torment that will befall them, or the Day of Resurrection, on the assumption that "فِي يَوْمٍ" (fi yawmin, "on a day") is dependent on "واقِعٍ" (waqi'in, "about to befall"). ﴿Far﴾, that is, they deem it far off by way of impossibility (al-ihalah, the judgment that something is impossible), and for this reason they ask about it mockingly.

﴿And We see it as near﴾: easy within Our power, not distant from Us or out of reach, with nearness and distance judged in relation to possibility. The clause is a causal explanation (ta'lil) for the command to be patient, and His, exalted is He, statement:

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 70, verse 8:**

﴿On the Day when the sky will be like molten brass﴾. It is connected (*mut'alliq*, the element governed or dependent on another word) to "near", meaning: it is possible, and no one will be able to make an excuse on that Day. Or it is connected to an implied element (*mudmar*, a word understood but not stated) indicated by "will occur" (*waqi'*). Or it is connected to a delayed implied element, meaning: "On the Day when the sky will be like molten brass... etc.," there will be among the states and terrors what cannot be described. Or it is a substitute (*badal*, a word that replaces and restates another) for "on a Day" (*fi yawm*), on the assumption that it is connected to "will occur." This is what they have said. Perhaps the closer view is that His saying, "A questioner asked," is a report of their familiar question, in the manner of His saying, ﴿They ask you about the Hour﴾, His saying, ﴿And they say, "When is this promise?"﴾, and similar verses, since it is the question that is commonly asked by the disbelievers, not what al-Nadr or Abu Jahl al-Fihri supplicated for. So the question has the meaning of asking, and the *ba'* (the preposition "with/about") has the meaning of "about," as in His saying, ﴿So ask about Him one who is informed﴾, and His saying, ﴿There is none to repel it﴾... etc. It is a resumptive statement (*isti'naf*, a new sentence that begins anew) brought to explain that the thing asked about will certainly occur. His saying, "So be patient with gracious patience," is consequent upon it. His saying, ﴿Indeed they see it as distant, but We see it as near﴾, is a reason for the command to be patient, as has been mentioned. His saying, ﴿On the Day when it will be...﴾ etc., is connected to "there is none to repel it," or to what it indicates, meaning: it will occur on the Day when the sky (p-31) will be like molten brass, which is what has been melted over a fire from metals, and it has been said: the dregs of oil.

﴿And the mountains will be like wool﴾: like wool dyed in various colours, because the mountains differ in colour. Among them are white and red streaks (judad) of differing hues, and jet-black ones (gharabib sud). Then, when they are crumbled (bussat) and set flying through the air, they resemble carded wool (al-'ihn al-manfush, dyed wool) when the wind scatters it.

﴿And no intimate friend will ask after an intimate friend﴾. That is: no relative will ask a relative about his circumstances or speak to him, because each of them is occupied with a trial that distracts him from that. It was also recited as قُرِئَ, with the verb in the passive form (عَلى البِناءِ لِلْمَفْعُولِ, "the passive voice"), meaning: no intimate friend is asked by an intimate friend, or his condition is not asked about from him.

﴿They will be made to see one another.﴾ That is, the close ones (al-ahibba') see their close ones (al-ahimma'), so none of them is hidden from the others. What prevents them from asking after one another is their preoccupation with their own condition. It was also said: what they see of each other's state suffices for them, such as the whiteness and blackness of the faces. The first view is more effective in conveying the terror. The two pronouns are in the plural to cover all close relations (al-hamim). It was also read as (يُبْصِرُونَهُمْ), with the verb in the active voice, meaning "they see them." The sentence is an independent resumptive clause (isti'naf, a new sentence that begins a fresh statement).

﴿The criminal would wish﴾ That is, the disbeliever would wish. It was also said: every sinner. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿if only he could ransom himself from the punishment of that Day﴾, means: the punishment with which they will be tested on that Day.

﴿with his sons﴾

Quranic quotations are in ﴿ ﴾. Translate the passage.

﴿And his wife and his brother﴾, expressing their desire, even if only in the sense of wishing (tamanni). It has been said: it is in the position of ʾan (that) in the nasb sense, so it has no response clause (jawab). From it and what follows it, a verbal noun (masdar) is formed that occurs as the object (maf'ul) of yawaddu (he would wish), and the implied meaning is: he would wish to ransom himself with his sons... etc. The sentence is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) explaining that the preoccupation of each guilty person with himself has reached the point where he wishes to ransom himself with the closest people to him and dearest to his heart, let alone caring about his condition and asking about it. It was also read: (yawma'idhin) with fatha, based on its being built (bina') because it is attached to a non-declinable (ghayr mutamakkin) noun, and with tanwin on (adhab) and the accusative of "yawma'idhin", its governing element being "adhab", because it carries the meaning of "punishment" (ta'dhib).

﴿And his kinsfolk (fasilatihi)﴾: that is, his clan, which he was separated from (fussila 'anhum).

﴿That shelters him (tu'wihi)﴾: that is, that gathers him in with respect to lineage, or at times of hardship.

Translation:

﴿And whoever is on the earth, all of them﴾ — from the two weighty ones (al-thaqalan: humankind and jinn) and the (other) creatures; and "man" (man, "whoever") is used here for predominance (al-taghlib: giving precedence to the rational beings).

﴿Then it would deliver him﴾ — this is coordinated (ʿataf) upon "yaftadi" (he would ransom himself), meaning: he would wish that he might ransom himself, and then that the ransom would deliver him. "Thumma" (then) here indicates the improbability (istibʿad) of the deliverance; that is: he wishes that all of these were under his control and that he had given them up as a ransom for his own self, and then that this would deliver him — but far, far from it (wa-hayhata: a word expressing remote improbability).

ﷺ

﴿Kalla﴾ (by no means): a rebuke to the criminal for his wish to be ransomed, and a declaration that deliverance through ransom is impossible. The pronoun in "innaha" (indeed it) either refers to the Fire, which is implied by the mention of the punishment, or it is an ambiguous pronoun (mubham) whose referent is explained by the predicate that follows, which is His, the Exalted's, statement: ﴿Laza﴾ (the Blaze). It is a proper name for the Fire, derived from al-laza (لظى), meaning: the flame (al-lahab).

(p-32)

{Nazza'atan lil-shawa} is in the accusative, either as a particularization (ikhtisas) or as an emphatic circumstantial clause (hal mu'akkida). Al-shawa means the extremities, or it is the plural of shawah, which is the scalp (jildat al-ra's). It was also read as {nazza'atun} with the nominative, as a second predicate (khabar thani), since {innaha} is the predicate, and {laza} is a substitute (badal) for the pronoun, or the pronoun refers to the matter (lil-qissa), and {laza} is the subject (mubtada') with {nazza'atan} as its predicate (khabar).

"Tad'u" (﴿تَدْعُو﴾): i.e., it draws [them] and brings [them] forward. It is said: it calls and says to them, "Come to me, come to me, O disbeliever, O hypocrite." It is also said: it calls the hypocrites and the disbelievers with an eloquent tongue, then snatches them up as a grain-picker snatches grains. It is also said: "tad'u" means it destroys. It is also said: it calls its guardians (zabaniyah).

﴿Man adbara﴾: i.e., turned away from the truth.

﴿Wa tawalla﴾: turned away from obedience.

Here is the translation:

﴿And gathered [wealth] and hoarded it﴾. That is: he gathered wealth and put it into a container and stored it up, did not pay its zakat and its dues, preoccupied himself with it away from the religion, and took pride in acquiring it out of greed and wishful expectation.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 70, verse 19:

﴿Indeed, mankind was created anxious (hala'an).﴾ Al-Hala' (anxiety, impatience): quick distress upon touching something disliked, and quick withholding upon touching good. The best explanation of it is the statement of the Most High:

﴿When evil touches him﴾, that is: poverty, sickness and the like.

﴿he is anxious﴾, that is: excessively anxious, given much to it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 70, verse 21:

﴿And when good touches him﴾ i.e., abundance and health.

﴿withholding﴾ exceedingly stingy and miserly. The three attributes are states that are either hypothetical or actual, since they are dispositions with which man has been created. The first "idhā" (when) is an adverbial clause modifying "jazū'an" (anxious), and the second is modifying "manū'an" (withholding).

Except those who pray (ﷺ)... 

Wait, I should translate faithfully without adding anything. Here is the translation:

﴿Except those who pray﴾ is an exception for those who are characterized by the sublime attributes that come later, from among those who were stamped with the blameworthy traits mentioned before; because their attributes indicate absorption in obedience to the Truth, compassion toward creation, belief in recompense, fear of punishment, breaking of desire, and preferring the Hereafter over the present life, in contrast to the blameworthy traits mentioned, which arise from being immersed in love of the present life and limiting one's gaze to it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 70, verse 23:

﴿Those who are constant in their prayer,﴾ nothing distracts them from it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 70, verse 24:

﴿And those in whose wealth there is a known right﴾ That is: a specified share which they make binding upon themselves, seeking nearness to Allah, the Exalted, and out of compassion for people, beyond the obligatory zakat (zakah) and the prescribed charities (sadaqat).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 70, verse 25:

﴿For the beggar﴾, the one who asks him.

﴿And the deprived﴾, the one who does not ask him, so he is thought to be rich and therefore is deprived.

Translation of the passage:

﴿And those who affirm the Day of Judgment﴾ i.e., by their deeds, in that they exert themselves in acts of obedience, bodily and financial, out of hope for the reward of the Hereafter, such that this is taken as evidence of their affirmation of the Day of Recompense.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 70, verse 27:

﴿And those who are apprehensive of the punishment of their Lord﴾ — fearful for themselves, even though they have good deeds, considering them few and magnifying His majesty, glorified and exalted is He, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who give what they give while their hearts are fearful that they will return to their Lord﴾, and His saying, exalted is He:

Verse 28: ﴿Indeed, the punishment of their Lord is not something to feel secure from.﴾ This is an interjection (i'tiraḍ) indicating that no one should feel secure from the punishment of Allah, the Exalted, even if he has gone to great lengths in obedience.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 70, verses 29–30:

﴿And those who guard their private parts,﴾ ﴿except from their wives or those their right hands possess, for they are not blameworthy.﴾ Its explanation has already passed in Surat al-Mu'minun.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 70, verses 29–30:

﴿And those who guard their private parts,﴾ ﴿except from their wives or those their right hands possess, for they are not blameworthy.﴾ Its explanation has already passed in Surat al-Mu'minun.

﴿Whoever seeks beyond that﴾ i.e., seeks for himself (what lies beyond that).

﴿beyond that﴾ beyond what has been mentioned, namely the spouses and the slave women.

﴿those are they﴾ the ones who seek (beyond that).

﴿they are the transgressors﴾ those who exceed the limits set by Allah Most High.

Here is the translation:

﴿And those who are, to their trusts and their covenant, keeping [watch]﴾. They do not neglect anything of their rights.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 70, verse 33:

﴿And those who are upright in their testimonies﴾. That is: those who establish them with justice, keeping alive the rights of people. Its being singled out for mention, although it is included within the trusts (amanat), is to make manifest its excellence. It has also been recited as (li-amanatihim) and (bi-shahadatihim), with the intent of the genus.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 70, verse 34:

﴿And those who are, over their prayer, ever-maintaining﴾ i.e., they observe its conditions (shara'it), and they perfect its obligatory acts (fara'id), its sunnas (sunan), its recommended acts (mustahabbat), and its etiquettes (adab). (p-34) The repetition of the mention of prayer, and the describing of them with it at the beginning and at the end, under two aspects, serves to indicate its excellence and its preeminence over all other acts of worship; and the repetition of the relative pronouns (al-mawsulat) serves to place the difference of attributes in the position of the difference of essences, as in the saying of the one who said:

"To the sovereign lord, the son of the lofty-minded, and the lion of battalions in the press of the crowd"

signifying that each one of the mentioned attributes is a distinguished quality in its own right, possessing a weighty standing that entails numerous rulings, and deserving to be assigned a separate, independent subject, and that none of them should be made a complement of another.

Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 70, verse 35:

﴿Those﴾ is a demonstrative referring to those described by the attributes mentioned, and the sense of distance contained in it, despite the nearness of the time of those indicated, serves to signal the elevated status of these people and the great distance of their rank in excellence. It is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is ﴿in gardens﴾, meaning: they abide in gardens whose extent cannot be measured and whose true nature cannot be grasped. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿honored﴾, is another predicate. Or it is the predicate, and "in gardens" is related to it, placed before it for the sake of observing the rhyme endings (fawasil). Or it is related to an implied verb that serves as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in the predicate, meaning: honored, existing in gardens.

"So what is the matter with those who disbelieve, rushing toward you" — "qibalaka" means "around you" (ḥawlaka).

"Muhti'īn" means hastening toward you, stretching out their necks toward you, and turning their eyes fixedly upon you.

"Abu al-Su'ud's commentary (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 70, verse 37:

﴿From the right and from the left, in groups﴾ That is: scattered groups. It is the plural of ʿizah (ʿizah, a group), and its root is ʿizwah, from al-ʿazw (ʿazw, attribution or belonging), as if each group attributes itself to other than that to which the other group attributes itself. The polytheists used to gather around the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in circles, circle after circle and group after group, mocking his speech, peace be upon him, and saying: "If these people enter Paradise as Muhammad says, then we will surely enter it before them." So this verse was revealed.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 70, verse 38:

﴿Does every one of them hope to be admitted into a Garden of bliss?﴾ Without faith.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 70, verse 39:

﴿Nay⦆ — a rebuke to them for that vain greed. ﴿Indeed, We created them from what they know﴾. It has been said: this is a causal explanation of the rebuke, and the meaning is: "We created them for the sake of what they know," as in the verse of al-A'sha:

"Have you resolved to depart from the household of Layla in haste, and has it become far for one who is smitten to be visited?"

It refers to perfecting the soul through faith and obedience. Whoever does not perfect it in this way is far from being placed in the station of the perfected; so how could they hope to enter the Garden, while they are bent upon disbelief, wickedness, and denial of the Resurrection? It has also been said that its meaning is: "We created them from what they know, namely a foul drop of semen; so how can they take pride, claim precedence, and say: 'We will surely enter the Garden before them'?" And it has been said: they were created from a filthy drop that is not suited to the world of holiness, so when it does not perfect itself in faith and obedience, nor adorn itself with the qualities of the angelic realm, it does not become fit to enter it. There is no concealing the far-fetchedness in all of these, and the closest view is that this is a resumed statement, which preceded as a preparation for what follows of the demonstration of His power, exalted is He, to destroy them for their disbelief in the Resurrection and the Recompense, (p-35) and for their mockery of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and of what was revealed to him, and their claim to enter the Garden by way of derision, and to bring in others in their place. For His power, exalted is He, over the creation they know of, the first creation, is a clear proof of His power, exalted is He, over that, as the eloquent fa' in His words, exalted is He, makes clear:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 70, verse 40:

﴿So I swear by the Lord of the easts and the wests﴾ The meaning is: since the matter is as He mentioned, that We created them from what they know, then I swear by the Lord of the easts and the wests.

﴿Indeed, We are able﴾

"Upon Our replacing them with better than them" — that is, We would utterly destroy them as their misdeeds require, and bring in place of them other creatures who are not of their description.

"And We are not to be outdone" — that is, not overcome, if We wished to do that. But Our will, which is founded on consummate wisdom, has required the postponement of their punishments.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 70, verse 42:

﴿So leave them﴾: let them be and their affair (fa-khallihim wa-sha'nahum).

﴿to plunge (yakhudu)﴾: in their falsehood (batilihim), of which among its components is what was related about them.

﴿and to play (yal'abu)﴾: in their worldly life (dunyahum).

﴿until they encounter their day which they are promised﴾: and it is the Day of Resurrection (yawm al-ba'th), at the second blast of the Trumpet (al-nafkhah al-thaniyah), not the day of the first blast (al-nafkhah al-ula) as it has been imagined (tuwuhhima), for the Exalted's saying:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 70, verse 43:

﴿On the Day they emerge from the graves⁠—﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "their day" (yawmihim). It is also read as "yukhrajūn" (they are brought out), in the passive voice, from the causative (ikhraj).

﴿Hastening⁠﻿—﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject-pronoun of "yakhrujūn" (they emerge), meaning: hastening.

﴿As though they were rushing to a target⁠—﴾ "Nusub" is everything that is set up and then worshipped besides Allah the Exalted. It is also read with a sukun on the ṣād, and with a fatḥah on the nūn and a sukun on the ṣād as well.

﴿Racing headlong⁠—﴾ means: they hasten.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 70, verse 44:

﴿Their eyes will be downcast﴾. Their eyes are described as downcast, though this is a description of the whole (person), owing to the extent to which the traces of it are evident in them.

﴿Humiliation will cover them﴾. A severe humiliation will overwhelm them.

﴿That﴾: that which has been mentioned, namely the terrifying conditions that will befall them in it.

﴿The Day that they were promised﴾: in this world.

From the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever recites the surah 'Sa'ala sa'il' (the Surah of the Questioner), Allah the Exalted will grant him the reward of those who are faithful to their trusts and their covenant."
